rainford_forces_next_slide.pptx.shape: question on one slide, answer on the next

pairs.q: What is the unit of force?
pairs.a: The newton (N)

pairs.q: What is weight?
pairs.a: The force acting on an object due to gravity

pairs.q: Write the equation that links weight, mass and gravitational field strength.
pairs.a: Weight = mass × gravitational field strength (W = mg)

pairs.q: What is the gravitational field strength on Earth?
pairs.a: 9.8 N/kg

pairs.q: What is a resultant force?
pairs.a: The single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting on an object

pairs.q: What happens to a stationary object when the resultant force on it is zero?
pairs.a: It stays stationary

pairs.q: What is friction?
pairs.a: A force that opposes motion between two surfaces in contact

pairs.q: What is a contact force?
pairs.a: A force that acts only when objects are touching

pairs.q: Give an example of a non-contact force.
pairs.a: Gravitational, magnetic or electrostatic force

pairs.q: What is the difference between mass and weight?
pairs.a: Mass is the amount of matter and is measured in kg; weight is a force measured in N

pairs.q: What is air resistance?
pairs.a: A frictional force that acts on an object moving through air

pairs.q: Write the equation linking work done, force and distance.
pairs.a: Work done = force × distance (W = Fs)

pairs.q: What is the unit of work done?
pairs.a: The joule (J)

pairs.q: What does Hooke's law state?
pairs.a: The extension of a spring is directly proportional to the force applied, up to the limit of proportionality

pairs.q: Write the equation for the force on a spring.
pairs.a: Force = spring constant × extension (F = ke)

pairs.q: What is a vector quantity?
pairs.a: A quantity that has both magnitude and direction

pairs.q: What is a scalar quantity?
pairs.a: A quantity that has magnitude only

pairs.q: Is velocity a scalar or a vector?
pairs.a: A vector

pairs.q: What is terminal velocity?
pairs.a: The constant velocity reached when the resultant force on a falling object is zero

pairs.q: What does Newton's first law state?
pairs.a: An object stays at rest or moves at constant velocity unless a resultant force acts on it

pairs.q: What is the function of the nucleus?
pairs.a: It contains genetic material and controls the activities of the cell

pairs.q: What is the function of the cell membrane?
pairs.a: It controls what enters and leaves the cell

pairs.q: Where does aerobic respiration take place?
pairs.a: In the mitochondria

pairs.q: What is the function of ribosomes?
pairs.a: They are where protein synthesis takes place

pairs.q: Name two structures found in plant cells but not animal cells.
pairs.a: Cell wall and chloroplasts (also a permanent vacuole)

pairs.q: What is the cell wall made of in plants?
pairs.a: Cellulose

pairs.q: What happens in chloroplasts?
pairs.a: Photosynthesis

pairs.q: What type of cell has no nucleus: prokaryotic or eukaryotic?
pairs.a: Prokaryotic

acids_red_answers.pptx.shape: answers in red/bold on the same slide

pairs.q: What is the pH of a neutral solution?
Which ion makes a solution acidic?
pairs.a: Hydrogen ions, H+

pairs.q: Which ion makes a solution alkaline?
pairs.a: Hydroxide ions, OH-

pairs.q: What is produced when an acid reacts with an alkali?
pairs.a: A salt and water

pairs.q: Name the salt made when hydrochloric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide.
pairs.a: Sodium chloride

pairs.q: What gas is produced when an acid reacts with a metal carbonate?
pairs.a: Carbon dioxide

pairs.q: What is the formula of sulfuric acid?
pairs.a: H2SO4

pairs.q: What colour is universal indicator in a strong acid?
pairs.a: Red

em_spectrum_with_class_list.pptx.shape: pupil names that must be ignored; one-row tables

pairs.q: What is the speed of light in a vacuum?
Name the part of the electromagnetic spectrum with the longest wavelength.
pairs.a: Radio waves

pairs.q: Which electromagnetic waves are used to cook food?
pairs.a: Microwaves

pairs.q: Which electromagnetic waves are used in remote controls?
pairs.a: Infrared

pairs.q: Which electromagnetic waves can cause skin cancer?
pairs.a: Ultraviolet

pairs.q: Which electromagnetic waves are used to image broken bones?
pairs.a: X-rays

pairs.q: Name the energy store in a stretched spring.
pairs.a: Elastic potential energy store

pairs.q: Name the energy store of a moving object.
pairs.a: Kinetic energy store

pairs.q: What is the unit of energy?
pairs.a: The joule (J)

pairs.q: What does the law of conservation of energy state?
pairs.a: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred

pairs.q: What is power?
pairs.a: The rate at which energy is transferred

pairs.q: What is the unit of power?
pairs.a: The watt (W)

pairs.q: Write the equation for efficiency.
pairs.a: Efficiency = useful output energy ÷ total input energy

pairs.q: What happens to wasted energy?
pairs.a: It is dissipated to the surroundings, usually as heat

pairs.q: How can unwanted energy transfer be reduced in a machine?
pairs.a: By lubrication

pairs.q: Name a renewable energy resource.
pairs.a: Wind, solar, tidal, hydroelectric, geothermal or biomass

pairs.q: Name a non-renewable energy resource.
pairs.a: Coal, oil, gas or nuclear fuel

pairs.q: What is the gravitational potential energy store?
pairs.a: The energy an object has because of its position in a gravitational field

pairs.q: What is the relative charge of a proton?
What is the relative charge of an electron?
What is the relative charge of a neutron?
Where are protons and neutrons found in an atom?
pairs.a: In the nucleus

pairs.q: What is the atomic number of an element?
pairs.a: The number of protons in an atom

pairs.q: What is the mass number?
pairs.a: The total number of protons and neutrons

pairs.q: What are isotopes?
pairs.a: Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons

pairs.q: Who discovered the electron?
pairs.a: J.J. Thomson

pairs.q: What did the alpha particle scattering experiment show?
pairs.a: That the mass of an atom is concentrated in a small positive nucleus

pairs.q: How many electrons fit in the first shell?

ecology_qa_lines.pdf.shape: Q:/A: lines in a text pdf

pairs.q: What is a habitat?
pairs.a: The place where an organism lives

pairs.q: What is a population?
pairs.a: All the organisms of one species living in a habitat

pairs.q: What is a community?
pairs.a: All the populations of different species living in a habitat

pairs.q: What is an ecosystem?
pairs.a: The interaction of a community of living organisms with the non-living parts of their environment

pairs.q: What is a producer?
pairs.a: An organism that makes its own food, usually by photosynthesis

pairs.q: What is a biotic factor?
pairs.a: A living factor that affects a community

pairs.q: Give an example of an abiotic factor.
pairs.a: Light intensity, temperature, moisture, soil pH or wind

pairs.q: What does a quadrat measure?
pairs.a: The number of organisms in a small sample area

pairs.q: What is interdependence?
pairs.a: When species in a community depend on each other for food, shelter, pollination or seed dispersal

pairs.q: What do decomposers do?
pairs.a: They break down dead organisms and return nutrients to the soil

transport_scanned.pdf.shape: scanned pdf (image only, question line then answer line)

pairs.q: What is diffusion?
pairs.a: The spreading out of particles from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration

pairs.q: What is osmosis?
pairs.a: The diffusion of water through a partially permeable membrane

pairs.q: What is active transport?
pairs.a: The movement of substances against a concentration gradient using energy from respiration

pairs.q: Where is the energy for active transport released?
pairs.a: In respiration

pairs.q: What is a partially permeable membrane?
pairs.a: A membrane that lets some molecules through but not others

pairs.q: Which process moves mineral ions into root hair cells?
pairs.a: Active transport

pairs.q: Give one factor that increases the rate of diffusion.
pairs.a: A bigger concentration gradient, higher temperature or larger surface area

pairs.q: What happens to an animal cell placed in pure water?
pairs.a: It swells and may burst

pairs.q: Conductor
pairs.a: A material that allows electric current to flow through it easily

pairs.q: Insulator
pairs.a: A material that does not allow electric current to flow through it easily

pairs.q: Current
pairs.a: The rate of flow of electric charge

pairs.q: Potential difference
pairs.a: The energy transferred per unit charge between two points

pairs.q: Resistance
pairs.a: How much a component opposes the flow of current

pairs.q: Series circuit
pairs.a: A circuit with only one loop

pairs.q: Parallel circuit
pairs.a: A circuit with more than one loop

pairs.q: Ammeter
pairs.a: A meter that measures current, connected in series

pairs.q: What is the chemical symbol for sodium?
pairs.a: Na

pairs.q: What is the chemical symbol for iron?
pairs.a: Fe

pairs.q: What is the chemical symbol for potassium?
pairs.a: K

pairs.q: What is the formula of water?
pairs.a: H2O

pairs.q: What is the formula of carbon dioxide?
pairs.a: CO2

pairs.q: What is an element?
pairs.a: A substance made of only one type of atom

pairs.q: What is a compound?
pairs.a: A substance made of two or more elements chemically joined

pairs.q: What is a mixture?
pairs.a: Two or more substances that are not chemically joined

pairs.q: How can you separate an insoluble solid from a liquid?
pairs.a: Filtration

pairs.q: How can you separate a soluble solid from a solution?
pairs.a: Crystallisation or evaporation

pairs.q: What does chromatography separate?
pairs.a: Mixtures of soluble substances, such as dyes in an ink

pairs.q: How can you separate two liquids with different boiling points?
pairs.a: Fractional distillation

pairs.q: What is the formula of methane?
pairs.a: CH4

pairs.q: What is the formula of sodium chloride?
pairs.a: NaCl

pairs.q: What gas relights a glowing splint?
pairs.a: Oxygen

pairs.q: Wavelength
pairs.a: The distance from a point on one wave to the same point on the next wave

pairs.q: Amplitude
pairs.a: The maximum displacement of a point on a wave from its rest position

pairs.q: Frequency
pairs.a: The number of waves passing a point each second

pairs.q: Period
pairs.a: The time taken for one complete wave to pass a point

pairs.q: Transverse wave
pairs.a: A wave where the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer

pairs.q: Longitudinal wave
pairs.a: A wave where the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer

pairs.q: Hertz
pairs.a: The unit of frequency

pairs.q: Reflection
pairs.a: When a wave bounces off a surface

pairs.q: Refraction
pairs.a: When a wave changes direction as it passes from one medium into another

pairs.q: Wave speed
pairs.a: Frequency × wavelength
